subject: Biology
generalObjectives: demonstrate sufficient knowledge of the concepts of the diversity, interdependence and unity of life;
account for continuity of life through reorganization, inheritance and evolution;
apply biological principles and concepts to everyday life, especially to matters affecting living things, individual, society, the environment, community health and the economy.

topics.title: Living organisms
contents: a. Characteristics
b. Cell structure and functions of cell components

c. Level of organization: (i) Cell e.g. euglena and paramecium; (ii) Tissue e.g. epithelial tissues and hydra; (iii) Organ e.g. onion bulb; (iv) Systems e.g. reproductive, digestive and excretory; (v) Organisms e.g. Chlamydomonas.
objectives: differentiate between the characteristics of living and non-living things;
identify the structures of plant and animal cells;
analyse the functions of the components of plant and animal cells;
compare and contrast the structure of plant and animal cells;
trace the levels of organization among organisms in their logical sequence in relation to the five levels of organization of living organisms.

topics.title: Evolution among Organisms
contents: a. Monera (prokaryotes), e.g. bacteria and blue green algae.
b. Protista (protozoans and protophyta), e.g. Amoeba, Euglena and Paramecium.
c. Fungi, e.g. mushroom and Rhizopus.

d. Plantae (plants): (i) Thallophyta (e.g. Spirogyra); (ii) Bryophyta (mosses and liverworts) e.g. Brachmenium and Marchantia; (iii) Pteridophyta (ferns) e.g. Dryopteris; (iv) Spermatophyta (Gymnospermae e.g. cycads, conifers; Angiospermae monocots e.g. maize, dicots e.g. water leaf); (v) Plants classified on the span of their life cycles.

e. Animalia (animals): (i) Invertebrates (coelenterates e.g. Hydra, Platyhelminthes flatworms e.g. Taenia, Nematoda roundworms, Annelida e.g. earthworm, Arthropoda e.g. mosquito, cockroach, housefly, bee, butterfly, Mollusca e.g. snails); (ii) Multicellular animals / vertebrates (pisces, amphibia, reptilia, aves, mammalia).
objectives: analyse external features and characteristics of the listed organisms;
apply knowledge to demonstrate increase in structural complexity;
trace the stages in the life histories of the listed organisms;
apply knowledge of life histories to demonstrate gradual transition from life in water to life on land;
trace the evolution of the listed plants;
trace the advancement of the invertebrate animals;
determine the economic importance of the insects studied;
assess their values to the environment;
classify plants into annuals, biennials and perennials;
trace the advancement of multi-cellular animals;
determine their economic importance.

topics.title: Structural/functional and behavioural adaptations of organisms
contents: a. Adaptive colouration and its functions (countershading in fish, toads, snakes and warning colouration in mushrooms).
b. Behavioural adaptations in social animals (castes in termites and bees, basking in lizards, hibernation and aestivation).

c. Structural adaptations in organisms: obtaining food (beaks/legs of birds, insect mouthparts); protection and defence (stick insects, praying mantis, toad); securing mates (Agama lizards, bird feathers); regulating body temperature (skin, feathers, hairs); conserving water (spines, scales).
objectives: describe how the various structures, functions and behaviour adapt these organisms to their environment, and way of life;
categorize countershading in fish, toads, snakes and warning colouration in mushrooms;
differentiate various castes in social insects like termites and their functions in their colony hive;
account for basking in lizards, territorial behaviour of other animals under unfavourable conditions (hibernation and aestivation);
account for adaptation in organisms with respect to food gathering, protection/defence, securing mates, temperature regulation, and water conservation.

topics.title: Internal structure of a flowering plant and mammal
contents: a. Internal structure of a flowering plant: (i) Root, (ii) Stem, (iii) Leaf.
b. Internal structure of a mammal: Internal organs (digestive, reproductive, excretory).
objectives: identify the transverse sections of these organs;
relate the structure of these organs to their functions;
identify supporting tissues in plants (collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem and phloem fibres);
describe the distribution of supporting tissues in roots, stem and leaf;
examine the arrangement of the mammalian internal organs;
describe the appearance and position of the digestive, reproductive and excretory organs.

topics.title: Nutrition
contents: a. Modes of nutrition: (i) Autotrophic, (ii) Heterotrophic.
b. Types of Nutrition: holozoic, parasitic, saprophytic, carnivorous plants.
c. Plant nutrition: (i) Photosynthesis (light and dark reactions, necessities), (ii) Chemosynthesis, (iii) Mineral requirements (macro and micro-nutrients).

d. Animal nutrition: (i) Classes of food substances, (ii) Food tests, (iii) Mammalian tooth (structures, types, dental formulae), (iv) Mammalian alimentary canal & accessory organs, (v) Nutrition process (ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation, enzymes).
objectives: compare autotrophic and heterotrophic modes of nutrition;
provide examples from both flowering and non-flowering plants;
compare the photosynthetic and chemosynthetic modes of nutrition;
differentiate heterotrophic feeding forms (holozoic, parasitic, saprophytic, carnivorous);
differentiate the light and dark reactions of photosynthesis;
determine the necessity of light, carbon (IV) oxide and chlorophyll in photosynthesis;
detect the presence of starch in a leaf as evidence of photosynthesis;
identify macro- and micro-elements required by plants and their deficiency symptoms;
indicate sources, nutritional value, and deficiency diseases of food classes;
determine the importance of a balanced diet;
detect the presence of a food type from experiment results;
describe tooth structure, differentiate types and dental formulae in man, sheep and dog;
relate structure of alimentary canal and accessory organs to functions;
identify digestive enzyme characteristics, substrates and end products.

topics.title: Transport
contents: a. Need for transportation.
b. Materials for transportation (excretory products, gases, manufactured food, digested food, nutrient, water, hormones).
c. Channels for transportation: (i) Mammalian circulatory system (heart, arteries, veins, capillaries); (ii) Plant vascular system (phloem and xylem).
d. Media and processes: cytoplasm, cell sap, blood, lymph; diffusion, osmosis, plasmolysis, turgidity, transpiration pull, root pressure, active transport.
objectives: determine relationship between increase in size/complexity and need for transport system;
determine sources and transport forms of materials;
describe circulatory system and functions of major blood vessels;
identify organs and functions of plant vascular system (xylem, phloem);
state composition and functions of blood and lymph;
describe diffusion, osmosis, plasmolysis and turgidity;
compare transport mechanisms in animals and plants.

topics.title: Respiration
contents: a. Respiratory organs and surfaces.
b. Mechanism of gaseous exchange in plants and animals.
c. Aerobic respiration (glycolysis, Krebs cycle, ATP production).
d. Anaerobic respiration (fermentation, role and economic importance of yeast, oxygen debt in muscles).
objectives: explain the significance of respiration;
describe outline of chemical processes in glycolysis and Krebs cycle with ATP production;
deduce gaseous exchange and heat energy production from experiments;
describe respiratory organs and surfaces across organisms (body surface, gill, trachea, lungs, stomata, lenticels);
describe mechanism for opening and closing of stomata;
examine the role of oxygen and consequences of insufficient oxygen in muscles;
demonstrate fermentation using yeast and state economic importance of yeasts.

topics.title: Excretion
contents: a. Types of excretory structures: contractile vacuole, flame cell, nephridium, Malpighian tubule, kidney, stoma and lenticel.
b. Excretory mechanisms: kidneys, lungs, skin.
c. Excretory products of plants: carbon (IV) oxide, oxygen, tannins, resins, gums, mucilage, alkaloids.
objectives: define and state significance of excretion;
relate characteristics of excretory structures with functions;
relate structure of kidneys to excretory and osmo-regulatory functions;
identify functions and excretory products of lungs and skin;
deduce economic importance of plant excretory products.

topics.title: Support and movement
contents: a. Tropic, tactic, nastic and sleep movements in plants; role of auxins.
b. Supporting tissues in animals (chitin, cartilage, bone).
c. Types and functions of skeleton: exoskeleton, endoskeleton; joints and mammalian skeletal layout.
objectives: determine need for support and movement in organisms;
identify supporting tissues in plants and their distribution;
relate plant responses to stimuli (light, water, gravity, touch) and auxin roles;
relate location of chitin, cartilage and bone to supporting function;
relate mammalian skeletal structure to supportive, locomotive and respiratory functions;
differentiate types of joints using appropriate examples.

topics.title: Reproduction
contents: a. Asexual reproduction: fission, budding, natural and artificial vegetative propagation.
b. Sexual reproduction in flowering plants: floral parts, pollination, fertilization, fruit/seed formation, placentation.
c. Reproduction in mammals: reproductive organs, fertilization, embryonic development, maternal health, IVF and birth control.
objectives: differentiate between asexual and sexual reproduction;
apply natural and artificial vegetative propagation methods in agriculture;
relate floral parts to functions, pollination and fertilization;
state advantages of cross pollination;
deduce types of placentation and fruit types;
differentiate male and female mammalian reproductive organs and gamete fusion;
relate maternal health and drug effects on embryonic development;
explain modern methods of regulating reproduction (IVF, contraception).

topics.title: Growth
contents: a. Meaning of growth.
b. Germination of seeds and conditions necessary (epigeal and hypogeal germination).
objectives: apply knowledge of conditions necessary for germination on plant growth;
differentiate between epigeal and hypogeal germination.

topics.title: Co-ordination and control
contents: a. Nervous coordination: CNS and PNS components, transmission of impulses, reflex actions and conditioned reflexes.
b. Sense organs: skin, nose, tongue, eye, ear; structures, functions, defects and corrections.
c. Hormonal control: animal endocrine glands (pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, pancreas, gonads); phytohormones (auxins, gibberellin, cytokinin, ethylene).
d. Homeostasis: body temperature regulation, osmoregulation (salt and water regulation).
objectives: apply knowledge of CNS and PNS in body coordination;
illustrate reflex actions and differentiate voluntary vs involuntary/conditioned reflexes;
relate sense organs to functions and corrections of defects;
state locations and functions of endocrine glands and hormones in animals and plants;
relate role of hormones in homeostasis (temperature, water, salt balance).

topics.title: Factors affecting the distribution of Organisms
contents: i. Abiotic factors: temperature, rainfall, relative humidity, wind, altitude, salinity, turbidity, pH, edaphic conditions; measuring instruments (secchi disc, thermometer, rain gauge).
ii. Biotic factors: activities of plants and animals, human impact.
objectives: relate effects of abiotic factors on organism distribution;
use appropriate equipment to measure abiotic factors;
describe how activities of plants and animals affect distribution.

topics.title: Symbiotic interactions of plants and animals
contents: a. Energy flow in ecosystem: food chains, food webs, trophic levels.
b. Nutrient cycling in nature: carbon cycle (global warming, gas balance), water cycle, nitrogen cycle (bacteria and legumes).
objectives: determine examples of symbiosis (parasitism, saprophytism, commensalism, mutualism, amensalism, competition, predation, cooperation);
explain distribution with food chains and webs;
describe carbon, water, and nitrogen cycles.

topics.title: Natural Habitats
contents: a. Aquatic: ponds, streams, lakes, seashores, mangrove swamps.
b. Terrestrial/arboreal: tree-tops, abandoned farmland, savanna fields, burrows/holes.
objectives: associate plants and animals with aquatic and terrestrial habitats;
relate adaptive features to habitats.

topics.title: Local (Nigerian) Biomes
contents: Tropical rainforest, Guinea savanna (southern and northern), Sudan savanna, Desert, Montane highlands (Obudu, Jos, Mambilla Plateaus).
objectives: locate biomes in Nigerian regions;
apply knowledge of biome features to determine regional characteristics.

topics.title: The Ecology of Populations
contents: a. Population density and overcrowding.
b. Adaptation for survival: competition factors, intra- and inter-specific competition, niche differentiation.
c. Factors affecting population sizes: biotic and abiotic factors.
d. Ecological succession: primary and secondary succession to climax community.
objectives: determine reasons for rapid human population changes and overcrowding consequences;
calculate population density per unit area;
relate population pressure with competition and succession;
determine interactions between biotic and abiotic factors;
trace sequence in ecological succession to climax stage.

topics.title: Soil
contents: a. Characteristics of soil types (sandy, loamy, clayey): structure, porosity, capillarity, humus content.
b. Components: inorganic, organic, soil organisms, soil air, soil water.
c. Soil fertility: loss of fertility, renewal, conservation methods (contour ridging, terracing, mulching, crop rotation, fertilizers).
objectives: identify physical properties and measure particle size, porosity, water retention;
determine air, water, humus, capillarity experimentally;
relate soil characteristics to healthy plant growth;
relate degradation factors to fertility loss;
apply soil conservation practices to maintain fertility.

topics.title: Humans and Environment
contents: a. Diseases: common endemic and epidemic diseases (malaria, meningitis, schistosomiasis, onchocerciasis, typhoid, cholera, polio, TB, STIs); vectors and prevention.
b. Drug abuse: addiction, commonly abused drugs, effects on health.
c. Pollution and control: air, water, soil pollutants; sanitation and sewage disposal.
d. Conservation of natural resources: renewable and non-renewable, desertification prevention, conservation agencies (NCF, Federal Ministry, National Parks, WWF, IUCN, UNEP).
e. Game reserves and National parks in Nigeria.
objectives: identify ecological conditions favouring disease spread and vector biology;
apply principles of vaccination and inoculation on disease control;
define drug abuse and identify commonly abused drugs and health effects;
categorize pollution and determine control methods;
explain sanitation importance in community health;
assess roles of health agencies (WHO, UNICEF, IRCS);
apply conservation methods and identify conservation bodies and reserves in Nigeria.

topics.title: Variation In Population
contents: a. Morphological variations: size, colour patterns, fingerprints.
b. Physiological variations: tongue rolling, PTC tasting, ABO blood groups.
c. Applications of discontinuous variation in crime detection, blood transfusion, and paternity determination.
objectives: differentiate between continuous and discontinuous variations with examples;
relate environment and genetic constitution to variation;
measure and plot frequency distributions of continuous traits;
apply fingerprints classification in identity detection;
identify and categorize physiological variations;
apply blood grouping knowledge to transfusion, paternity, and forensics.

topics.title: Heredity
contents: a. Inheritance of characters: heritable and non-heritable traits.
b. Chromosomes – the basis of heredity: DNA structure, transmission of traits, segregation and recombination during meiosis and fertilization.
c. Probability in genetics and sex determination.
d. Applications: agriculture (cross-breeding, in-breeding, out-breeding), medicine (counseling, sickle cell, Rhesus factor).
e. Sex-linked characters: baldness, haemophilia, colour blindness.
objectives: determine heritable and non-heritable traits with examples;
illustrate simple structure of DNA;
illustrate segregation and recombination of genes at meiosis and fertilization;
analyze cross-breeding experiment data;
apply principles of heredity in crop and livestock improvement;
analyze contentious issues in GMO, gene therapy, biosafety;
apply heredity in marriage counseling (sickle cell, Rhesus);
identify characters that are sex-linked.

topics.title: Biotechnology
contents: Applications of biotechnology in agriculture, medicine (recombinant DNA, insulin, interferon, enzymes), pharmaceuticals, and food industry.
objectives: define biotechnology;
describe significance of recombinant DNA materials in medicine;
list applications in agriculture, medicine, pharmaceuticals, and food industries.

topics.title: Theories of evolution
contents: Lamarck’s theory, Darwin’s theory, organic evolution theory.
objectives: relate organic evolution to adaptive changes resulting in organism diversity;
explain the contributions of Lamarck and Darwin to evolutionary theory.

topics.title: Evidence of evolution
contents: Evidences from fossil records, comparative anatomy, physiology, embryology, genetics, and mutation.
objectives: state evidences in support of organic evolution;
mention evidences from fossils, comparative anatomy, physiology, and embryology;
trace evolutionary trends in plants and animals;
state evidence from modern genetic studies and role of mutation.
